The paper presents computational evidence from molecular dynamics simulations of a size-dependent power law relationship between the critical resolved shear stress (CRSS) for edge dislocation motion and the volume fraction of γ' precipitates in nickel superalloys.
The CRSS exhibits two distinct power law regimes separated by a critical precipitate size of around 120 Å, which corresponds to the total core width of paired dislocations in the γ' phase.
The two-regime power law behavior of CRSS with volume fraction of γ' precipitates is found to be independent of temperature over the range of 300-700 K studied.
The CRSS is found to have a linear relationship with the length of the γ' precipitate along the direction of dislocation motion, with the two regimes separated by the 120 Å critical length scale.

For small precipitates (< 120 Å), the variations in the total and inner core widths of the paired dislocations are more dramatic as they pass through the precipitate, while for larger precipitates, these variations become less significant.
Simulations with spherical precipitates also show a similar two-regime power law behavior of CRSS with precipitate diameter, with the transition occurring at a diameter of around 120 Å.
The power law exponent of around 1/3 suggests that the CRSS has a linear dependence on the length of the γ' precipitate along the direction of dislocation motion.
The dislocation velocities in the γ and γ' phases are found to be similar, with the velocity in the γ phase being slightly higher than in the γ' phase.

The key strengthening mechanisms in nickel superalloys that are influenced by the γ' precipitates include chemical strengthening, stacking fault strengthening, modulus strengthening, coherency strain strengthening, and order strengthening.
The current study is limited to simulations with γ' precipitates having the same orientation as the γ matrix, and future research should explore the effects of different relative orientations.
The interplay between precipitate size, distribution, and other factors on the dislocation-precipitate interactions warrants further investigation.
The results presented in this work highlight non-trivial size-dependent effects and provide new details on the strengthening effect of γ' precipitates in nickel superalloys.
The findings have important implications for larger-scale dislocation dynamics studies and alloy design for nickel superalloys.
The molecular dynamics simulations used in this study complement experimental limitations in spatial and temporal resolution for studying dislocation-precipitate interactions.

Prior experimental and computational studies have explored dislocation-precipitate interactions in nickel superalloys, but the size-dependent power law behavior reported in this work has not been previously observed.
